summary: Psalm 142 is a short prayer from a speaker who feels trapped, hunted, and abandoned. The speaker pours out complaint before Yahweh, says no human refuge remains, and asks to be delivered from stronger persecutors. The psalm ends with hope that rescue will lead to thanks and renewed company among the righteous.
whyItMatters: This chapter shows the Psalter making room for prayer from isolation and danger, not only from calm confidence. In Book V, it joins the larger movement toward praise while still preserving the voice of someone not yet delivered.

context.author: The heading associates the psalm with David, but such headings can indicate authorship, association, dedication, or belonging, and their exact historical force is debated.
context.audience: Israel's worshiping and instructed community, later adopted by Jewish and Christian communities for public prayer and private life.
context.date: The Psalms are an anthology formed over time; this chapter should not be assigned a precise date from its wording and heading alone.
context.setting: The heading says, “when he was in the cave,” while the poem itself speaks from overwhelming trouble, hidden danger, abandonment, and a plea for rescue.
context.literaryForm: Hebrew poetic prayer of distress, using direct address to Yahweh, complaint, petition, and anticipated thanksgiving.

outline.heading: The prayer begins aloud
outline.note: The heading identifies the psalm as a contemplation and prayer associated with David in the cave; the speaker cries to Yahweh and asks for mercy.

outline.heading: Complaint poured out
outline.note: The speaker openly brings complaint and troubles before God.

outline.heading: Overwhelmed and watched by God
outline.note: The speaker says his spirit was overwhelmed, yet God knew his route while enemies hid a snare on his path.

outline.heading: No human refuge
outline.note: The speaker asks God to look beside him and see that he has no concerned helper, no refuge, and no one who cares for his soul.

outline.heading: Yahweh named as refuge
outline.note: The speaker turns directly to Yahweh and confesses him as refuge and portion in the land of the living.

outline.heading: Deliverance requested
outline.note: The speaker asks Yahweh to listen and deliver him from persecutors who are too strong for him.

outline.heading: Rescue and thanks anticipated
outline.note: The final petition asks for release from prison so the speaker may give thanks, expecting the righteous to surround him because of Yahweh's goodness.

keyVerses.text: I pour out my complaint before him. I tell him my troubles.
keyVerses.why: This verse states the action of the psalm: distress is spoken directly before God rather than hidden or softened.

keyVerses.text: Look on my right, and see; for there is no one who is concerned for me. Refuge has fled from me. No one cares for my soul.
keyVerses.why: This is the chapter's clearest statement of abandonment and loss of human support.

keyVerses.text: I cried to you, Yahweh. I said, “You are my refuge, my portion in the land of the living.”
keyVerses.why: The prayer turns from failed refuge elsewhere to Yahweh as the speaker's refuge and portion.

keyVerses.text: Bring my soul out of prison, that I may give thanks to your name. The righteous will surround me, for you will be good to me.
keyVerses.why: The final verse holds together the plea for rescue, the promised thanksgiving, and the hope of restored community.

questions.question: What kind of psalm is this?
questions.answer: Psalm 142 is a prayer of distress. The speaker cries for mercy, describes trouble and isolation, asks for deliverance, and looks toward thanksgiving if rescued. It is not a calm reflection from safety; it speaks from need.

questions.question: Does the heading prove David wrote this in a specific cave?
questions.answer: The heading says the psalm is “by David” and places it “when he was in the cave.” Psalm headings are ancient parts of the received Psalter, but their grammar can mark authorship, association, dedication, or belonging. Readers differ over how much historical certainty such headings provide, so the heading should guide the reading without making details beyond the text certain.

questions.question: What does “A contemplation” mean here?
questions.answer: “A contemplation” appears in the heading as a label for the psalm. The chapter does not explain the term further. For a first reading, it is safest to notice that the heading gives a type label and that the poem itself functions as “A Prayer.”

questions.question: Is it wrong for the speaker to bring a complaint to God?
questions.answer: The chapter presents complaint as something the speaker brings before Yahweh: “I pour out my complaint before him.” It does not treat honest distress as outside prayer. The psalm shows trouble being voiced directly to God rather than denied.

questions.question: What does it mean that God knew the speaker's route?
questions.answer: Verse 3 contrasts the speaker's overwhelmed spirit and hidden danger with God's knowledge: “you knew my route.” The text does not say the danger is imaginary; it says a snare has been hidden on the path. The point within the verse is that God knows the speaker's way when the speaker is overwhelmed and threatened.

questions.question: Why does the speaker say no one is concerned for him?
questions.answer: Verse 4 describes complete social abandonment: no one is concerned, refuge has fled, and no one cares for the speaker's soul. The language may be poetic and intense, but the psalm asks readers to feel the isolation as part of the trouble. The chapter does not identify the people who failed him.

questions.question: What does “my portion in the land of the living” mean?
questions.answer: The speaker calls Yahweh “my refuge, my portion in the land of the living.” In this verse, “portion” names what the speaker claims as his sustaining share when other refuge has disappeared. The phrase stays tied to life in this world, since the verse says “in the land of the living.”

questions.question: Who are the persecutors?
questions.answer: The chapter does not name them. It only says they are “too strong for me,” and earlier says “they have hidden a snare for me.” They may be concrete enemies within the poem's situation, but the chapter text does not let us identify them more precisely.

questions.question: Does “Bring my soul out of prison” mean the speaker is literally in jail?
questions.answer: Readers differ. The line can be read as a plea for release from literal confinement, especially alongside the heading's cave setting, or as poetic language for being trapped by danger and distress. The chapter itself does not describe bars, guards, or a formal prison; it does describe desperate need, persecutors, and loss of refuge.

glossary.def: Compassion or help asked from Yahweh at the start of the prayer.
The speaker's spoken grievance and distress, poured out before God rather than kept hidden.
A trap hidden on the speaker's path, used here for danger prepared by enemies.
A place or source of safety; the speaker says human refuge has fled but calls Yahweh his refuge.
The speaker's claimed share or sustaining possession, used here for Yahweh in the land of the living.
